lead: This unit explains what a Geographic Information System is, how it stores the earth as layers, and how it turns those layers into answers. After it you can name the parts of a GIS, choose between raster and vector for a task, plan a data input and checking routine, and run a buffer and overlay to pick a site or map a hazard.
about: The unit moves from what a GIS is to what it can do. Chapter 7.1 defines GIS and its five parts. Chapter 7.2 separates the two halves of every GIS record, location and attribute. Chapter 7.3 shows the two ways of storing location, raster and vector, with their costs. Chapter 7.4 covers getting map and field data in, cleaning it and proving it is fit to use. Chapter 7.5, taught in only a few universities, places every layer on the earth through a datum and a projection. Chapter 7.6, also advanced, combines layers by overlay and distance to produce a suitability or risk map. Applications run throughout: drought, school siting, construction monitoring and flood mapping.

chapters.idea: A GIS is an organised system of five parts that captures, stores, analyses and displays spatially referenced data to answer questions, not just software that draws maps.
chapters.depth: Define GIS with the five components: hardware, software, data, people, methods or procedures. Some syllabi write 'Geographical Information System', others 'Geospatial Information System'. Give the four functions: data input, storage and management, manipulation and analysis, output. Contrast GIS with CAD (drawing), with a plain database (no location), with remote sensing (a data source) and with digital mapping (display only) — the difference is location-based analysis. History in brief: the 1960s Canada Land Inventory work of Roger Tomlinson, the Harvard graphics laboratory of the same decade, the shift from mainframe to desktop in the 1980s, then web and cloud GIS. Indian context: Bhuvan and other ISRO/NRSC geoportals, Survey of India digital topographic data, and location data in everyday phone apps. Name the syllabus applications in one line each: drought management, GIS-based planning of rural schools, extraction of building attributes, zonal planning with remote sensing, and civil engineering use.

figure.title: GIS at work
figure.aria: A flow diagram running from spatial data through input, storage, analysis and output to a decision, with analysis marked out.
figure.caption: The marked analysis step is where a GIS does more than colour a map.

chapters.example: A city engineer must find every street within 200 m of a proposed metro station that has no water main. Three layers exist: street centre lines, water mains, and the station point. Worked answer: (1) input and check the three layers — input component; (2) buffer the station point at 200 m — analysis component; (3) clip the street layer to that buffer — analysis; (4) select water mains, buffer them by the pipe width, and erase that from the streets — analysis; (5) the leftover streets are the answer; plot them on a ward map — output; (6) the engineer decides the new pipe route — people.
chapters.trap: Writing 'GIS = Google Maps', 'GIS = satellite image' or 'GIS = mapping software'. The exam wants a system with five components and four functions, and the analysis step named as the difference from digital mapping.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for maps, scales and topographic sheets; Unit 6 for what a remote sensing image supplies.
chapters.leave: Raster and vector details to 7.3, projections to 7.5, overlay operations to 7.6, image processing to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Every GIS feature carries two kinds of information joined by a key: where it is (spatial data) and what it is (attribute data).
chapters.depth: Spatial data: position in a stated coordinate system, plus shape, size, orientation and topology. Name the primitives — point, line, polygon, surface — and note that the same object can be all three at different scales (a town is a point on a national map, a polygon on a district map). Define topology as the stored neighbour relations: adjacency, containment, connectivity. Continuous fields (elevation, temperature) versus discrete objects (wells, parcels). Attribute data: a table of records (rows, features) and fields (columns, properties). Measurement scales: nominal (soil type, road class name), ordinal (condition rank 1 to 5), interval (temperature in °C), ratio (length in m, population). Say which operations each scale allows. Primary key links the table to the geometry; a join merges two tables on a shared key, one-to-one or one-to-many. Distinguish an attribute query ('all bore wells deeper than 60 m') from a spatial query ('all wells inside ward 7'). Metadata: source, date, scale, accuracy, owner.

figure.title: Attribute table of four tube wells
figure.aria: A five-row table in which the first two rows hold coordinates and the last three rows hold attributes, for four wells shown as columns one to four.
figure.caption: Rows one and two are the spatial half; the last three rows are the attribute half.

chapters.example: Four tube wells are surveyed: Well 1 at easting 412 m, northing 1330 m, open type, depth 40 m, ward 7; Well 2 at 415, 1332, open, 55 m, ward 7; Well 3 at 418, 1328, bore, 80 m, ward 9; Well 4 at 421, 1331, bore, 65 m, ward 9. Worked questions: (a) the depth field is a ratio scale, the type field is nominal, because depth has a true zero and type has no order; (b) attribute query 'depth > 60 m' returns Wells 3 and 4; (c) spatial query 'inside ward 7' returns Wells 1 and 2; (d) the ward number is the key that joins this table to the ward boundary table, and the join is many-to-one.
chapters.trap: Calling the coordinate columns 'attributes'. Coordinates are the spatial half; the table of properties is the attribute half. Also forgetting that a join needs a common key of the same type, so ward '07' will not join to ward 7.
chapters.prereq: 7.1; Unit 1 for coordinate and scale ideas.
chapters.leave: How the geometry is physically stored to 7.3; how coordinates are projected to 7.5.

chapters.idea: The same ground reality can be stored as pixels on a grid (raster) or as points, lines and polygons with coordinates (vector), and each choice trades detail against storage and analysis ease.
chapters.depth: Vector model: point, line (arc, made of vertices), polygon (closed chain of vertices); nodes where lines meet; topology stored as arc-node and polygon-arc lists. Some syllabi call this the feature-based or object-based model. List advantages: sharp boundaries, small storage for sparse data, exact lengths and areas, good for networks and parcels. Disadvantages: complex overlay, poor for continuous fields, topology maintenance. Raster model: a grid of cells (pixels) in rows and columns, with an origin, a cell size and one value per cell. Some syllabi call it the cell-based or grid-based model. Cell value can be elevation (a DEM), land cover class, or a photograph band. List advantages: simple overlay and map algebra, good for continuous surfaces, easy with remote sensing images. Disadvantages: blocky boundaries, large storage, resolution fixed at input. Storage estimate: rows × columns × bits per cell ÷ 8 gives bytes. Mention the TIN in one line as a vector surface of triangles, and note conversion both ways (rasterising, vectorising) in one line. Close with a comparison table on boundary sharpness, storage, overlay, network analysis and source.

figure.title: Raster grid, cell size 20 m
figure.aria: A three by four grid of elevation values in metres, with the four cells at or above 35 metres marked.
figure.caption: The marked cells are ground at or above 35 m; the whole grid covers 4 800 m².

chapters.example: A 3 × 4 raster of elevation covers a plot; the cell size is 20 m and the values in metres are row 1: 22, 25, 31, 34; row 2: 24, 29, 35, 38; row 3: 27, 33, 41, 45. Worked questions: (a) area of one cell = 20 × 20 = 400 m²; (b) total raster area = 12 cells × 400 = 4 800 m²; (c) cells at or above 35 m are 35, 38, 41, 45, so four cells; (d) high ground area = 4 × 400 = 1 600 m²; (e) a well at a single point and a pipeline as a line belong in the vector model, while the elevation surface belongs in raster.
chapters.trap: Saying raster always means a photograph and vector is always more accurate. Raster accuracy is set by cell size at input; a 30 m grid cannot show a 5 m road. Also forgetting that the area of a raster feature is cell count × cell area, not a drawn polygon area.
chapters.prereq: 7.2 for the geometry and attribute split; Unit 6 for resolution of images.
chapters.leave: Spatial, spectral and radiometric resolution to Unit 6; projection of the grid to 7.5; overlay of grids to 7.6.

chapters.idea: Data must be converted into the chosen model, cleaned of geometric and attribute errors, and then checked against independent evidence before any analysis is trusted.
chapters.depth: Sources: existing paper maps and toposheets, total station and GNSS observations, remote sensing images, scanned documents, spreadsheets, crowdsourced points. Input methods: manual digitising on a table, on-screen (heads-up) digitising over a scanned or georeferenced image, scanning plus vectorising, coordinate geometry (COGO) entry from survey records, direct import of total station and GNSS files, and image interpretation. Cover georeferencing: control points with known coordinates, a transformation, and a residual at each point. Editing: snapping to nodes, adding and deleting vertices, splitting and merging lines, trimming overshoots, filling gaps, closing polygons, deleting duplicate nodes, removing slivers. Build topology and test for dangles, undershoots and unclosed polygons. Enter attributes with the correct type, domain and key, and avoid duplicate records. Verification and quality: positional accuracy from control-point residuals, attribute accuracy against a field sample, logical consistency, completeness, edge matching between adjacent sheets, and metadata. Manipulation in brief: transformation, rubber sheeting, edge matching, clipping, format conversion, merging.

figure.title: From map sheet to clean layer
figure.aria: A flow diagram from source map through georeferencing, digitising, editing, topology building and attribute entry to verification, with editing and verification marked.
figure.caption: The marked edit step removes slivers and overshoots before attributes are attached, and the last step proves the layer against the field.

chapters.example: A toposheet is georeferenced on four control points. The residuals in metres are: point 1 (+2.0, +1.0), point 2 (−1.0, +2.0), point 3 (+1.0, −2.0), point 4 (−2.0, −1.0), given as (easting, northing). Worked answer: sum of squares in easting = 4 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 10, mean = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5; the same in northing gives 2.5; total RMS error = √(2.5 + 2.5) = √5 ≈ 2.24 m. A tolerance of 5 m is met, so the layer is accepted. During cleaning, 7 dangles, 3 slivers and 2 duplicate nodes are found; the polygons affected are rebuilt before attribute entry, because a sliver has no real owner and would split the area wrongly.
chapters.trap: Judging quality by how tidy the screen looks. Dangles, slivers and duplicate nodes look harmless and still break area and overlay results. Also mixing up digitising precision (how many decimals are stored) with positional accuracy (how close to the ground truth).
chapters.prereq: 7.2 and 7.3; Unit 1 for scales and map sheets; Unit 5 for total station and GNSS data capture.
chapters.leave: Image classification and enhancement to Unit 6; drone and SfM processing to Unit 5 and Unit 6; overlay operations to 7.6.

chapters.idea: Every layer must state the datum, projection and units that map the curved earth onto a flat coordinate plane, or features from different sources will not line up.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this unit; keep it short and concrete. Geographic coordinates: latitude and longitude in degrees, a position on the ellipsoid, no flat-plane distance. Projected coordinates: easting and northing in metres on a flat grid. Ellipsoid (a smooth mathematical earth), geoid (mean sea level surface), datum (an ellipsoid fixed to the earth, e.g. WGS84 or Everest). Projection families: cylindrical, conic, azimuthal; each preserves one property at the cost of others — shape (conformal), area (equal-area), distance or direction. Transverse Mercator and UTM: 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide, numbered from zone 1 at 180° W; a central meridian; a scale factor of 0.9996 on the central meridian; false easting 500 000 m; false northing 10 000 000 m in the southern hemisphere. India falls roughly in zones 42 to 47. On-the-fly reprojection in software and why it does not fix a wrong datum. Datum mismatch between WGS84 and an old Indian datum can shift features by hundreds of metres. State that Indian topographic sheets are prepared on the Everest ellipsoid and that the sheet margin names the projection, so check the margin rather than assume.

figure.aria: A stack of five nested definitions from coordinate system at the top down to the earth surface at the bottom.
figure.caption: Each level of the stack must be stated in the data; a mismatch at the datum level shifts every feature.

chapters.example: A point near Chennai is at 80° E, 13° N. Worked answer: (a) UTM zone number = floor((longitude + 180) ÷ 6) + 1 = floor(260 ÷ 6) + 1 = 43 + 1 = 44; (b) zone 44 runs from 78° E to 84° E, so its central meridian is 81° E; (c) the point is 1° west of that meridian; (d) the scale factor at the central meridian is 0.9996, so a 1 000 m line on the ground measures 999.6 m on the grid there, a 0.4 m difference in 1 km; (e) the false easting there is 500 000 m, so eastings in the zone never go negative. If the same point is entered as WGS84 in a layer built on the Everest datum, it moves by hundreds of metres on the map.
chapters.trap: Feeding degrees into software that expects metres, or assuming two layers with the same numbers share a datum. A projection cannot be chosen without knowing which property — area, shape, distance — the job needs.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for datums and coordinate systems; 7.3 for how coordinates are stored with the geometry.
chapters.leave: GNSS positioning methods and satellite geometry to Unit 5; area computation from coordinates to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: GIS earns its cost by combining layers — by proximity, overlay and reclassification — so that the output answers a sitting question that no single layer answers.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short and applied. Attribute query versus spatial query. Point-in-polygon selection and proximity: buffer at a stated distance, then dissolve to remove internal boundaries. Vector overlay: clip, erase, union, intersect, identity, symmetric difference, spatial join; state which keeps which attributes. Area rules: the intersect area is at most the smaller input, the union area is not the sum of the two. Raster map algebra: local (cell by cell), focal (neighbourhood such as slope), zonal (summarised per polygon), global (whole grid). Reclassification of a layer into scores, then weighted overlay with weights summing to 1 to give a suitability index. Slope and aspect from a DEM in one line. Spatial correlation: whether high values of one layer sit with high values of another. Applications named in the syllabi: drought management (rainfall, soil, crop layers), GIS-based planning of rural schools, extraction of building attributes, zonal planning with remote sensing, flood and landslide mapping, construction monitoring.

figure.title: Weighted overlay for a school site
figure.aria: Two input layers reclassified into scores, combined by a weighted overlay and turned into a suitability map, with the overlay step marked.
figure.caption: The marked step turns two separate scores into one suitability value per site.

chapters.example: Three villages are candidates for a new school. Two criteria are scored 1 to 5: child population within 2 km, weight 0.6; distance from the nearest existing school, weight 0.4. Village A scores 5 and 2 → 0.6 × 5 + 0.4 × 2 = 3.0 + 0.8 = 3.8. Village B scores 4 and 4 → 2.4 + 1.6 = 4.0. Village C scores 2 and 5 → 1.2 + 2.0 = 3.2. Village B is chosen. A 2 km buffer around an existing school covers π × 2 000² ≈ 12.57 million m², that is about 12.57 km²; in a 30 m raster the same buffer is about 13 963 cells, each 900 m². If a flood layer is intersected with the ward layer, the flooded area is smaller than either input, and the union area is not the sum of the two.
chapters.trap: Adding areas across a union, treating buffer distance as area, and forgetting that weights must sum to 1 and that a score of 5 is not comparable across layers unless the class breaks are stated.
chapters.prereq: 7.3 for raster and vector storage; 7.4 for clean topology; 7.5 so all layers share a datum and projection.
chapters.leave: Image classification as an input to the layers to Unit 6; drone DEM generation to Unit 5.
